target:
def Target : Prop :=
  ∀ (P D E R : Type) (t : S3 P D E R), t.D23 →
    ∀ w : P → E,
      (∀ r, t.D22 r → ∃ p, ∃ o ∈ t.c1 p, t.c3 o = r ∧ t.c4 r ≠ w p) ∨
      (∃ p, ∃ o ∈ t.c1 p, w p ∉ t.c2 o)

translation: Target names a proposition; it does not prove it. For every choice of types P, D, E, R and every record t of type S3 P D E R, use the following terminology. Call r in R realized if t.c3(o) = r for some o belonging to t.c1(p) for some p in P. Let A(r) be the set of all such p for r, and let B(p) be the union of t.c2(o) over all o in t.c1(p), without restricting t.c3(o). Assume that for every realized r there exist a function S from A(r) to A(r) and an element p of A(r) such that B(p) and B(S(p)) are disjoint. The disjointness is required only for the chosen p, and S(p) need not be distinct from p. Under this hypothesis, for every function w from P to E, at least one of the following holds: (1) for every realized r, there exist p in P and o in t.c1(p) such that t.c3(o) = r and t.c4(r) ≠ w(p); or (2) there exist p in P and o in t.c1(p) such that w(p) is not in t.c2(o). The disjunction is for each w as a whole, not separately for each r. In (1) the witnesses may depend on r; in (2) no condition on t.c3(o) or t.c4 is required.

divergences.description: The first disjunct requires one wrong inference for each realized content, not that every individual inference is wrong. For example, let two systems produce the same sole content r, have different true experiences, and each predict exactly its own true experience. Swapping the systems witnesses substitution. If the inference for r returns the first system's experience, Lean's first disjunct holds because of the second system, even though the first inference is correct and neither prediction is wrong.

As declared, Lean introduces an arbitrary truth assignment w that fixes one experience per system across all its datasets. It tests prediction error against w directly, without requiring a correct inference on the corresponding dataset to witness that error.

judgement.summary: The target matches the author's per-content formulation, but being wrong at least once for each content is weaker than the passage's claim that no single inference points at the correct experience.
